utterances.text: That is about how far from central Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some, around one-and-a-half to two kilometres until the beginning of Kozarusa and then somewhere around two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: About what time of the day was it that you stopped at or near Limenka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think around 10 o'clock, maybe 10.30, somewhere around there, the way I can remember as we started off from Mujici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were Serb forces there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What were those Serb forces wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they wore camouflage uniforms and they wore weapons, automatic rifles, pistols, knives. There were some bombs as well, some grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you and the other elderly people ordered off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we got off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you and the others wait after you got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the right-hand side, on the right of -- the bus came to a stop and it stopped next to the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you and the other elderly people wait by the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the Serb forces separating Muslim men from women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were some of the men being placed on buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, as you waited by the side of the road there at Limenka did you see Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Dule Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was he when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was passing by next to, by the bus from the left side. I saw Milos Balte and some others, those policemen that I knew from the earlier years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall what Dule was wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he had a camouflage uniform. They all had camouflage. Well, maybe some of the regular policemen had those police uniforms, but all the rest had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you and the other elderly people eventually put back on the same bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same bus, we were put on the same bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you then taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At Trnopolje were the newly arrived people told that those who had relatives or friends nearby could stay with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you and the members of your family go to a nearby relative's or friend's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first house next to the camp, the east, Ahmed Balic was the owner of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: About how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a larger structure with -- he said that he had over 50 people staying with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did it seem to you that that estimate was correct based upon the number of people you saw at the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that that is about the right number, maybe even more, but it is true what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the nationality of those people who were at Mr. Balic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there much food available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was food, but there was not enough. You know, he is a retiree. He did not have as much of that, what he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to obtain a certificate from the Serbian Red Cross which permitted you to leave the area in order to look for food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did get a certificate from Donlagici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Donlagici part of the Kamicani commune?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that certificate permit to you go to a part of Kamicani then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only to Donlagici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that the part of Kamicani in which your house was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Over the next two weeks, approximately, did you, nevertheless, go to your house in Kamicani in order to search for food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see cleansing taking place in the area of your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was happening there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were burning the houses and people were being killed, the ones who were left behind, the ones who were blind or old, and they were saying, "We were not guilty, why should I go somewhere? I am not guilty of anything", so those people got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a Serbian checkpoint in the area of Kamicani which was guarded by Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean a point? There was near the -- in Rodi Godina on the road Prijedor/Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the members of the Serbian forces who were manning that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to that point I was -- there were four Serbian soldiers in a car who caught up with me. They stopped me. He opened the door and he asked me, "Meho, where are you going?" I told him, "I am going home to search for food for my children. My children are hungry".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you discouraged from going there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me, he said that they were cleansing up there, "It is not safe, you, it is your initiative, but if you get caught you will get killed". However, I started and he told me, "Don't go to the checkpoint, they won't let you through", and this was about 30 metres from where they caught up with me. He said, "There are things going on up there". I was looking and I saw Milenko Zigic there and Vinko Kusota, Slavko Skondric, Milan Markovic and Milan's son-in-law, Gojko, and some others that I did not know, but these people I knew because these are my immediate neighbours. They are maybe 1.5 or two kilometres from me. So them I know as well as I know myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were those persons armed and were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody was in uniform, and wearing arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kind of arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Automatic weapons. It was all automatics. We have a saying, "They were armed up to their teeth".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Vinko Kusota. How long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him from ever, but I knew him best since '70. Vinko Kusota, he jumped off from a plum tree and he stabbed himself on a knife, and I was carrying, I was driving some rocks nearby and so when I heard screams I went over there and I saw the blood, and he was still a child so I took him, I put him on my cart and dropped by my house. I then took him to Kozarac, then to Prijedor. Then I found Drago Konjovoda. I know him as myself, and he had a small red -- a yellow Fiat which would take him to Banja Luka. So I gave him the money. I said, "Please take him" so I know him as I know myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, on your last trip, the fourth trip, to look for food at your house, were you stopped by Serb soldiers, seized and then taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on 10th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Omarska where were you first taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, they put us on the pista -- no, first, they took us up to the headquarters first, and up there they -- he went to the office. Then they put us up against a wall. We had two fingers there and that is how we stood there. There were three soldiers and they beat us. Those Serb soldiers, they beat us and they abused us. Then that one came back and said, "Go to pista and they will call you out and you will go there to be interrogated".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the beating were you slapped in the face and kicked in the groin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at first I was slapped on the face, and then with a rifle butt he hit me here and then he -- in the groin he kicked me because we had to have our legs spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you held after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I was on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many days were you held in the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there three nights and four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After that where were you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In room 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you remain in room 15, that is, did you remain held in room 15 until you were transferred to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on 26th August when they took me to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, did you say that was 26th August? What date was it that you were transferred to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6th August. On 26th we returned from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, may I ask you how you would describe the general conditions in Omarska during the time you were held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, the conditions that they were, I can hardly describe them, what I have seen during my 73 years, in '42 I was in a camp, in 1945 I was in a camp, but this camp, it is unimaginable. It is death of a camp, not a camp. One thing is a camp, another is a death of a camp and I cannot, I cannot imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were prisoners regularly called out of rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As far as you could tell, what happened to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for us, as I know, there were people who were taken out and then were beaten and beaten, and bring them in and he is dead. They just bring him in and throw him into the room. There were people who never even came back, who were called out and never returned and we -- to this day we do not know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the condition of prisoners who were held in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I did see. One night I saw when they took us out to have a bath, he had a hose like this one. We were stripped naked from room 15 and washed us with icy water, beating us. It was not really washing us. It was beating us on the head and on the face, and I saw there about 20 of them being taken from the white house, stripped of their clothes. They did not look like humans. They looked like black sheep or black horse, they were that black, and there was no way you could tell a part of a body. I mean, they were so beaten up. When I saw those people, I could not, I could not eat a piece of bread for two days and I was hungry, but those people, they left such an impression, I could not really -- I could never even think that people could do this thing to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the time you arrived in Ormaska, Mr. Alic, had you learned what had happened to your sons, Ekrem and Enver, or where they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about Ekrem while I was in Trnopolje, that Ekrem had been killed in Kozara, and it was the Omladinsko Naselje on Kozara, Benkovac, once upon a time it was called Srpski Benkovac and then Omladinsko Naselje, a youth brigade settlement that my son and my nephew had been killed there and so .....

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the time you arrived in Omarska did you know where Enver was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was on the pista I saw my Enver, when he passed by over me, he flew by me. I knew that he was there in the camp. When I came to the 15, somebody said, "Hey, Enver is calling to you. He is behind that room 15", but he was in another room behind the door, iron door, and we talked to each other. He asked me, "Where are the children, where were you? Where did they get you?" and I tell him, well, so and so. "I have heard that Eno had been killed and he says, "Father, yes" or "no" and that was it and .....

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So your son, Eno, asked you what had happened to Ekrem and you had to tell him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, after you came to room 15, was there a day when you were called from your room and ordered to fetch your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after, I think, after some four days or maybe five, I would not be able to pin point it, they came to the door and said, "Alic Mehmed nicknamed 'Meho', come out and find son Enver".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, before you were called out that day, on that particular day, had you seen Dule Tadic in camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Dule Tadic that day. When I went out to lunch and he was sitting with Meakic on the west side of the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the top of the hangar. When time for lunch came, there was always 30 people in the group and I was always the first one. I always headed it, the first one, as we moved there in a column and they always put me up front because I could not move very fast, my leg hurts a little, and besides I am of an age, you know, so they always said, "Come, Alic, you go first", so that I went first and I was at the corner of the pista and the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, can I ask you to take the pointer which should be to your right near that console? Perhaps Miss Sutherland can help you with that. Keep your headphones on, but in a moment I will ask you to take your headphones off, put on the headphones that they will give you at this desk and then I will ask you to point out on the model where you were and where Dule Tadic was when you saw him. So if you could remove your headphones and step up there, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you be able to see, Mr. Wladimiroff, do you think, or Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. If need be, either you or Mr. Kay, whoever will be handling cross-examination, may approach. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): Mr. Alic, can you first show us where Dule Tadic and Meakic were when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Tadic was here and I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you were at the corner of the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could ask you just once again to point out the corner where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right here. We came out through this door, walked here, and that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you could point out again where Dule Tadic was, his approximate position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Tadic here, at any rate from this side, from the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alic. You may take your seat again. What was Dule Tadic doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was sitting with Meakic. They were talking, conversing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall what Mr. Tadic was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage clothes too. I saw him on a couple of occasions. He always had camouflage clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he was clean shaven or had a beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, that, well, he was, what do I know, but with all this repression, with all this hurry, I could not really, you know, how to tell you. If you move your head a little, there is immediately a rifle butt against your back, so it was better to look after one's back and not to see everything, because in that war a man told me, "Don't see everything and don't hear everything". That was '45, 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see Dule Tadic on any other occasion in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Once again, I do not know how, I saw him on the east side standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the other side of the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the other side of the pista, on the east side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you or what were you doing when you saw him on that second occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day too, I was going for lunch. I did not see him otherwise because I never went anywhere. Only if I went to lunch I could see someone otherwise because they did not take me anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On both occasions were you able to look long enough to be absolutely sure that it was Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, it was always very quickly, but Dule Tadic is Dule Tadic. I know him. There may be 10 people like this and I will say which one is he, third, fourth, fifth or they may be moving in a column. I know him. I know his build like myself. There is no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all on this, how long after the time when you saw him with Meakic was it that you saw him on the other side of the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, about 20 days or so, what do I know? I do not know but I know that some time had passed by, and I saw that Kobas without an arm and I saw Meakic, that Drago, and I saw them there, a couple of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I ask you to point out with the pointer where Dule Tadic was on that second occasion you saw him. Perhaps you could extend it and you may be able to reach or if you need to get up, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was here. This is the garage and there is a tap, a water tap, or something like that. I poured it while I was on the pista. I came there to get some water to drink and I know it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On that first occasion when you saw Dule Tadic after lunch, did you return back to room 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Later that day did you hear the names of prisoners being called out from their rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day I heard this one calling out, Karabasic Emir, Jasko Hrnic, and some others were called out too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know those two men, Emir Karabasic and Jasko Hrnic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure I did. What do you mean? They were my sons' great friends, colleagues, what do I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you remember hearing them call out the name of your son, Enver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember they called out my son, but they called out me, for me to go and take my son out, to go and find him. He came to the door, "Alic, please, Alic Mehmed called Meho, go and find your son" and I came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, when you were first called out and an announcement was first made, did you respond immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know -- I tried to dodge it, not to respond. So he shouted, "Alic" once, he shouted "Alic" twice and the third time when he said, "Come out for your mother, he is the oldest in the room, I will recognise him, I will kill 20 men for him", but people told me, "Meho, come on, don't be crazy. You have to go". So I went out. A soldier was standing by the door holding an automatic rifle. I do not know that lad, he was blond but I did not know him really much, and he hit me with a rifle butt but not particularly well. I mean, one has to say the truth. He did not really hit me properly. So he told me, "Down the stairs" and I started down the stairs. I went down one stairs and then another. He said, "To the left", and I to the left, to the hangar. When I started in the direction of the WC to the right, so I started down the hangar to the right. On the right was the WC.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, how were you walking at that time? What position were you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to have our hands up there, like this, and the head down. But when I turned to the right I looked ahead of me and I saw Emir Karabasic in front of me sitting on a table like this, his feet dangling, and I saw he was bloody. When I drew nearer, I stopped for about 10, 15 per cent, and I saw him being cut all over with a knife and there were three soldiers to the right of him, in fact to the east of him, and he was right by the wall and they were to the east -- not to the east, to the north, towards the WC. As the water was poured over him and he was shaking, evidently he was stunned, and so they were trying to bring him to his senses back. Then I jolted badly, but a soldier shouted, "So you know him, well, you are going to know him, F your mother", and he put a knife, a soldier's knife, right up here, and the one going, walking behind me, hit me with a rifle butt here on the right side, in the kidneys, and this one jerked his knife and hit me on the head with the flat side of the knife, and then hit me here with the handle, and I still have a scar where he hit me with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you make an effort to see who those soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I thought I did, but I could not see since I had the knife here. There is not a man who can look around if there is a knife at his throat. Few people can do it and I am not -- I may be a man but I did not have guts to look around and I could not see them, who they were, what they were. But I do know that Dule Tadic was there and who else, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the man who was escorting you direct you toward Enver's room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went along towards the door where my son, Enver, was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you got to the room where the stairway upstairs is, were you told to go upstairs and get your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came near that door the guard opened and said, "Go upstairs", and the one who was following, who was escorting me, stayed there. So I went up the stairs. How I walked, I do not know. I was, sorry, I was lost. I knew where I was going, why I was going, what is happening, what was happening, and I found my son and he was like me, also shivering, "Son there, they say you have to come out". Then he says to me, "Father, I am not here, and maybe I am", he said. "No, I was told if we call you out once again, then you will be no more". Eno, my Eno, put on, somebody gave him a vest or something, a leather jacket, if they beat him so that it hurts him less. He got ready. We started. When we came downstairs they shouted, "Faster, faster". I was walking the first and Eno was following me. When we came down to the hangar, this one was waiting for me, another one was waiting for him, saying, "Why aren't you coming out for your mother?" So we made a move few steps, and said, "Lie down", and he went down on his stomach and with a right foot here, he kicked him on the left side once, twice, and he cried out of pain. You know that, how it is. I mean, he was a strong man, but -- I came back to my senses. I started wailing, screaming. I wanted to defend him somehow, to shield him, to ask them, but they told me, "Get lost. Get him. We shall cut his throat too". Those two grabbed him and he said to me, "Father, take care of my children, look after my children". I started to the left and on their right side I heard them shouting, "Dule, brother, how have I wronged you? Why do you beat me?" I heard them beating in the hangar. I passed that way towards the pista and that one escorted me across the pista upstairs to the office, left me in front of the door. He went inside and those there mistreated me again at the door. One hit me, then he started off. Then the other one shouted, "Leave him, let him be." He said, "Comrade, Commander, I have taken Eno Alic out. What shall we do with the old man?" He said, "Take him to the room from which you had taken him out". When I returned by the hangar the same way that I had come by, I heard wails and screams, cries out, cries, and I started up the stairs and I heard, he said, "This one's finished. I mean, mother, what are you going to make Ustasha with now?" He opened the door to me and I entered the room and they asked me, people asked me, "Meho, what is it?" and I said, "Brothers, I have lost my other son. They have killed my son". So that I -- I do not know what happened to me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, did you ever see your son Enver alive after that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never again from that day, never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, do you see Dule Tadic in court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you point him out, please, and tell us what he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you see him wearing, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has a green jacket and a tie, but I am not interested in him. A criminal -- I am not interested in a criminal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, we have just asked to you identify Mr. Tadic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The record will reflect the identification, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The record will reflect that the witness has identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, would it be right to say that Dusko Tadic was someone that you did not associate with in Kozarac because he was of a different generation to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: His father was more your generation and someone you would ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- have spent time with, rather than Dusko Tadic who was 30 years younger than you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had no common interests with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, with Dule I had no relationship at all, only my sons did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- sons being ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I knew him as a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- one of them certainly, approximately the same age, were his generation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my Ekrem was the same generation. They were peers. They were born the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You had no business dealings with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no business with him ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There were many people in Kozarac with whom your sons were friendly and they were popular people in Kozarac, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they did, yes. They made no difference between Serbs and Muslims and Croats. We had brotherhood and unity. That is how it used to be until '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what we had, and Dule Tadic, he grew up with them. I do not know that he was ever -- or had any problems with Muslims. They were ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You did not know that he had any such problems because he had been popular with your sons as your sons were popular with the people of different nationalities in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When this day happened that there was the attack on Kozarac and there was shelling, had you expected that to happen that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not. I did not reckon on it, I did not thought -- I did not think that it would end, Serbs, our former neighbours like Dule Tadic and Zigic and Vinko and such that they would do what has been done. I was surprised because I was there from the former Yugoslavia. I was 14 or 15. Then it was the NDH, and then it was throughout the modern Yugoslavia, and I was just a hard working man, a farmer. For me, Serbs were just like Muslims. I do not know what they had, what their intentions they had with us, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you been aware of the ultimatums that had been issued from Prijedor requesting the police in Kozarac to deliver up their weapons and other Muslim people to deliver up their weapons? Were you aware of what was happening just before the shelling took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I cannot answer that question. I am not a politician. I was never in politics, so I do not know anything. I am a farmer. I worked in agriculture and I have nothing to tell this or that. I was never a politician. I never was involved in politics. I was just sewing corn and gardening when Serbs were getting ready. They were preparing themselves. They were preparing themselves for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On that day, 26th May, when you and many others left your homes in that region to join the people who were moving through the Marsala Tita Street, did you have any idea ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- about what was going to happen to you? Did you have any knowledge at all of what any plans may be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know anything. I only knew that it was not going to be good. They surrounded us and then they started burning down houses. When the first shot was fired, the houses went up in flames and the whole -- Kozarac was burned down and so now we do not .....

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you came to that stage that you were with the other women, children, men being separated, did you know what was going to happen to you, where you were going to do go? Did you know what the plans were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ask any of those people who were around to say, "What is happening? Do you know where I am going?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I asked no questions. My wife was 75. I had a deaf, mute daughter, two small grandchildren. I was still fighting for them. I knew exactly what was going on, so I was just trying to save them. So I do not know what I am supposed to demonstrate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were put on that bus to go to Trnopolje, that was the first bus, you said, that was at the particular place where the division was happening, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember who told you that you were going on to that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not. A Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many Serb soldiers were there in this place near Limenka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not count them. I do not think anybody could count them. I do not think anybody dared count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there army vehicles there or was it just soldiers on foot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw military vehicles in Kozarac, but there was a lot of traffic and there was a column of civilians. They were all on the move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say that you were put on the first bus that took you to Trnopolje, were you then at the head of the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that, yes, ours was the first bus. I was in the first bus from those civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know if other people had been separated or moved on in this way at this place before you arrived there? Was there anything that indicated that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there were, but I do not know. I know what I experienced and what I saw and for the rest, I cannot. I could not really look around. I was watching my own family because at that time I was 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were at this place where the people were being put on to or separated into various groups, how long did you stay there at this place near Limenka? How long did that take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think between my place and the bus, it was about an hour. They unloaded us, to look over our things. There are weapons, bayonets. They went through our bags and .....

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were these soldiers who were searching your bags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb soldiers -- who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect what sort of uniform they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, camouflage uniforms. They were all kinds. Maybe I saw 15, 20 of them, but there were 100 or 150. I was not put up there to watch who was wearing what, what kind of a cap. I was a prisoner. I knew that I was -- my freedom was taken away from me and then I was just to bow my head and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say you had to bow your head, do you mean that it could have been dangerous for you to look around at these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. You just could not call the person by their name, you could not recognise him. You could not say, "Where are you, neighbour?" because your head would be off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there then that fear of violence that you and other people were aware of whilst you were being dealt with in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, and other people left and I do not know how many but .....

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment before I enter a new topic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10 a.m. (5.30 p.m.) (The court adjourned until the following day) 25
